quizzes.title: Checkpoint — What the Market Actually Is

questions.text: A stock closed at ₹500 and opens near ₹490 on its ex-dividend date after declaring a ₹10 dividend. What happened?
options: Value moved from the share price into the cash dividend — wealth is unchanged
The company issued new shares, diluting the price
questions.explanation: On the ex-date the buyer no longer gets the dividend, so the price adjusts down by roughly the dividend amount. Holders receive the ₹10 in cash — nothing is lost, value just changed form.

questions.text: You bought shares using MIS (intraday product) and forgot to square off. What happens?
options: The shares are delivered to your demat account
The position automatically converts to delivery for free
The broker force-closes the position around 3:15–3:20 PM and charges a penalty fee
The position carries over to the next trading day
questions.explanation: MIS positions must close the same day. If you don't square off, the broker's risk system auto-squares it off near session end and levies an auto-square-off charge.

questions.text: If the person who sold you shares defaults and never delivers them, who makes you whole?
options: The clearing corporation, which guarantees every trade
questions.explanation: The clearing corporation steps in as counterparty to every trade — this guarantee is why you never need to worry about who is on the other side.

questions.text: You place a limit buy order at ₹450 while the stock trades at ₹460. What happens?
options: It waits in the order book and executes only if price comes to ₹450 or lower
It converts to a market order at the close
questions.explanation: A limit order gives you price control but no execution guarantee — it sits in the order book until price reaches your limit or you cancel it.

questions.text: Roughly what does a ₹50,000 delivery trade (buy + later sell) cost in total charges with a discount broker?
questions.explanation: Brokerage may be ₹0 but STT (0.1% both sides), transaction charges, stamp duty, GST and the DP charge add to roughly ₹130 — your position must rise ~0.26% just to break even.

questions.text: How is profit from F&O trading taxed in India?
options: As non-speculative business income at your slab rate
questions.explanation: F&O income is non-speculative business income — taxed at slab rates, with losses eligible for set-off and carry-forward, and audit requirements at high turnover.

questions.text: Why do transaction costs matter far more to an intraday trader than an investor?
options: Intraday charges are higher per trade
Costs scale with trade frequency — a few hundred rupees a day compounds to tens of thousands a year
questions.explanation: Per-trade costs look tiny, but 3 round trips a day at ~₹80 each is roughly ₹60,000 a year on ₹50,000 capital — a structural hurdle the strategy must first out-earn.

questions.text: After a decline into a known support zone, a candle prints a long lower wick and closes near its high. What does this tell you?
options: Sellers are still in full control
Sellers pushed price down but buyers absorbed the selling and drove it back up — a hammer at a meaningful location
The stock will definitely rally tomorrow
questions.explanation: The long lower wick shows rejected lower prices: sellers tried, buyers won. At support after a downtrend this is a hammer — meaningful because of its location. It raises probability; it guarantees nothing.

questions.text: The exact same hammer candle appears in the middle of a directionless range. What is it worth?
options: The same as at support — a hammer is a hammer
Very little — a candle's meaning comes mostly from its location (levels and trend context)
It signals a breakout is coming
questions.explanation: Location is ~80% of a candle's meaning. The identical pattern at a watched support level and in the middle of nowhere are entirely different pieces of information.

questions.text: A doji (open ≈ close) forms after a long, steep uptrend. The best reading is:
options: Buyers remain dominant — add to longs
A stand-off between buyers and sellers — the trend may be tiring; watch the next candles
An immediate crash signal — short now
A data error in the chart
questions.explanation: A doji is indecision. After a strong trend it hints the dominant side is losing control — a warning to pay attention, not a standalone reversal signal.

questions.text: What distinguishes a believable breakout candle through resistance from a suspect one?
options: A wide body closing decisively beyond the level on high volume
Any candle whose wick pokes above the level
A gap at the open, regardless of close
questions.explanation: Real breakouts look convinced: a decisive close beyond the level with expanded participation. Thin pokes above that close back inside are what false breakouts look like.

questions.text: Why do support and resistance levels exist at all?
options: Exchanges enforce price floors and ceilings
Human memory and regret — buyers, missers, and trapped shorts all have orders anchored to the same prices
Algorithms are programmed to defend round numbers only
They don't — levels are an illusion
questions.explanation: Levels are coordination points of memory: proud buyers add, regretful missers wait there, trapped traders exit at breakeven. That clustered order flow is what makes the level real — and partly self-fulfilling.

questions.text: Resistance at ₹520 finally breaks and price rallies to ₹560. Price now returns to ₹520. What do you expect?
options: ₹520 acts as support — breakout buyers defend entries, missers get their second chance (role reversal)
questions.explanation: Broken resistance tends to become support. The retest of a broken level is one of the highest-quality entry locations in trading.

questions.text: An uptrend is objectively broken when:
options: Price closes red three days in a row
Price fails to make a new high AND then takes out the last higher low
questions.explanation: Trend structure is the definition: higher highs and higher lows. When the last higher low breaks, the structure itself has failed — no indicator required.

questions.text: A support level has been tested five times in quick succession, with bounces getting smaller. The likely outcome is:
options: It is now stronger than ever — buy the sixth test aggressively
It will hold forever — five tests prove it
It is weakening — each test consumes the resting buy orders, and grind-through breaks become likely
questions.explanation: Each test eats the buy orders sitting at the zone. Repeated rapid tests with shrinking bounces usually precede the level quietly giving way.

questions.text: A stock breaks out above a 3-month range on volume well below its recent average. Your read:
options: Suspect — low participation makes it a false-breakout candidate; wait for confirmation or the retest
questions.explanation: A breakout is a claim that demand overwhelmed supply; thin volume undermines the claim. Believable breakouts typically come on 2–3× average volume.

questions.text: RSI on a strongly trending stock has been above 70 for three weeks while price keeps rising. The correct interpretation:
options: 'Overbought' means rising fast — in strong uptrends RSI can stay elevated for long periods; the textbook sell rule loses money here
The uptrend must end within days
questions.explanation: RSI >70 measures fast ascent, not an imminent fall. Mechanically selling 'overbought' in trends is a well-documented way to fight strong markets.

questions.text: What is the correct reading order for any chart?
options: Trend structure → levels → volume → indicators last
questions.explanation: Structure and levels are the meal, indicators the seasoning. Starting with indicators is the classic beginner inversion — they are derivatives of the same price data.

questions.text: Price grinds to new highs while volume shrinks at each new high. This suggests:
options: Fewer participants at each new price — the trend is running on fumes
questions.explanation: Rising price on falling volume means the advance is attracting less money at each step — a classic caution sign, especially when paired with other warnings.

questions.text: Why does rising crude oil hurt Indian markets specifically?
options: India exports crude and loses revenue
India imports ~85% of its crude — costlier oil worsens the trade deficit, weakens the INR and feeds inflation
It doesn't — crude is irrelevant to equities
questions.explanation: The import bill flows through the currency, inflation and corporate margins (paints, aviation, tyres). Sustained expensive crude has historically coincided with Indian market stress.

questions.text: NIFTY makes a new all-time high, but the advance/decline ratio is negative and fewer stocks sit above their 200-DMA than a month ago. This is:
options: A narrow rally carried by heavyweights — fragile, a classic late-cycle warning
Proof the bull market will continue
Impossible — breadth always confirms the index
questions.explanation: Weighted indices can be dragged up by a handful of large stocks while the average stock declines. Breadth divergence like this has preceded most major tops.

questions.text: FIIs sold ₹2,000 cr today while DIIs bought ₹1,800 cr. The most useful takeaway:
options: One day is noise; watch the 20-day cumulative flows. SIP-driven DII buying is a structural stabilizer against FII exits
questions.explanation: Single-day flow data is noise; sustained multi-week one-sided flow is signal. Domestic SIP money has made post-2020 corrections shallower than the FII-selling headlines suggest.

questions.text: India VIX spikes above 25 during a sharp market fall. Historically this has often marked:
options: The beginning of a multi-year bear market, always
Panic that frequently occurs near durable bottoms — a time to be alert for opportunity, not to panic-sell
A signal to take maximum leverage immediately
questions.explanation: Elevated VIX = fear fully priced. Many durable bottoms have formed in high-VIX panics — use it to adjust aggression and expectations, not as a standalone buy trigger.

questions.text: Capital ₹2,00,000, risk 1% per trade. Entry ₹450, stop-loss ₹438. How many shares?
questions.explanation: Quantity = (Capital × Risk%) ÷ (Entry − Stop) = ₹2,000 ÷ ₹12 ≈ 166. Position size comes from the stop distance, never from conviction.

questions.text: A system wins 45% of the time with average win ₹3,000 and average loss ₹1,500. Its expectancy per trade is:
options: Negative — a 45% win rate always loses
questions.explanation: Expectancy = (Win% × AvgWin) − (Loss% × AvgLoss) = 1350 − 825 = +₹525. Win rate alone is meaningless; the win/loss size ratio completes the math.

questions.text: After a 50% drawdown, what gain is needed just to get back to breakeven?
questions.explanation: Losses are asymmetric: half your capital gone means the remainder must double. This is why survival — capping drawdowns — is the first strategy.

questions.text: You feel extremely confident about a trade. How should that affect position size?
options: Double the size — conviction is an edge
Not at all — size comes from the stop distance and the fixed risk %; feelings are not a sizing input
Skip the stop-loss since you're sure
questions.explanation: Confidence has no statistical edge, and 'sure things' fail regularly. The sizing formula exists precisely to protect you from your own conviction.

questions.text: What is the minimum evidence before trading a strategy with real money?
options: It worked on the last 3 trades you eyeballed
A hand-logged backtest of 50–100 historical setups with computed expectancy, then paper trading, then minimum-size live trading
One profitable week of paper trading
questions.explanation: Small samples lie. The protocol — 50–100 logged setups, computed statistics, paper trading, tiny live size — is what separates a tested system from a hunch.

questions.text: Which section of a written strategy document typically saves the most money?
options: The 'when NOT to trade' rules (events, regimes, max open positions)
questions.explanation: Most large losses come from trading in conditions the strategy was never designed for — results days, violent ranges, correlated overexposure. Explicit no-trade rules prevent them.

questions.text: Why must the strategy be written down before trading it?
options: Because once real money moves, the brain becomes a rationalization machine — calm pre-made rules beat adrenalized decisions
It doesn't need to be written
questions.explanation: In the moment, you will convince yourself of almost anything. The written document is the calm version of you overruling the emotional version.

questions.text: What does paper trading test — and NOT test?
options: It tests your process and rules in real time, but not your emotions — paper losses don't hurt
It tests emotions but not process
questions.explanation: Paper trading validates mechanics and discipline of process. The emotional layer only appears with real money — which is why the next step is live trading at minimum size.

questions.text: The maximum possible loss for an option BUYER is:
questions.explanation: A buyer holds a right, not an obligation — the worst case is the option expiring worthless, losing exactly the premium. Sellers carry the larger, potentially open-ended risk.

questions.text: You buy a call before quarterly results. The company beats estimates and the stock rises 2% — yet your option FALLS in value. Why?
options: IV crush — implied volatility was inflated before the event and collapsed after, outweighing the favourable move
questions.explanation: Event options price in big expected moves. When the event passes, that volatility premium deflates (vega loss). You must be right on direction, size AND timing to beat inflated IV.

questions.text: Theta measures:
options: The premium lost per day to time decay — accelerating near expiry; the seller's income, the buyer's cost
questions.explanation: Options are melting assets. A sideways week costs a buyer money while being 'not wrong' — and pays the seller. Decay accelerates in the final 1–2 weeks.

questions.text: Bull call spread: buy 22,000 call at ₹200, sell 22,200 call at ₹110. Max loss, max profit, breakeven?
questions.explanation: Net debit = 200 − 110 = ₹90 = max loss. Max profit = spread width (200) − net debit = ₹110, above 22,200. Breakeven = 22,000 + 90 = 22,090. Everything capped and known — the point of defined-risk structures.

questions.text: Why can heavy call open interest at a strike act like resistance?
options: SEBI blocks trading above such strikes
Option writers who sold those calls defend the strike — their hedging and interest create supply near it
questions.explanation: Writers of those calls profit if price stays below the strike and act (hedging, rolling, defending) in ways that add supply near it. Useful context — never a guarantee.

questions.text: Averaging down on a losing trade means you systematically have:
options: Maximum size in your worst-performing ideas and minimum size in your best
A lower average price, which is always good
Higher win rate with no downside
questions.explanation: Adding to losers concentrates capital precisely where the market is telling you you're wrong. The professional habit is the inverse: add only to winners.

questions.text: What should you grade yourself on weekly?
options: Rule-following (process adherence) — a rule-following loss is a good trade; a lucky rule-breaking win is a bad one
How you feel about the market
questions.explanation: You control process, not outcomes. Rewarding lucky rule-breaks trains your brain to gamble; the edge only expresses itself across a series of disciplined trades.

questions.text: The practical antidote to revenge trading is:
options: Trading bigger to win it back faster
A hard daily-loss limit — once hit, close the terminal
questions.explanation: After a loss the urge to 'win it back' produces oversized, low-quality trades. A pre-committed daily stop removes the decision from the heated moment.

questions.text: A company reports strong, growing profits, but operating cash flow is persistently far below reported profit. This is:
options: A classic red flag — profits are opinion, cash is fact; the divergence deserves investigation
questions.explanation: Earnings can be shaped by accounting choices; cash flow is much harder to fake. Sustained profit-vs-cash divergence has preceded many blowups.

questions.text: You study a list of today's most successful traders to learn their common habits. The main statistical trap is:
options: Survivorship bias — you can't see the many who used the same habits and went broke
questions.explanation: The losers with identical behaviours vanished from view. A large enough crowd flipping coins always produces a few 'geniuses' — Taleb's core point.

questions.text: Graham's 'margin of safety' means:
options: Buying far enough below your estimate of value that being partly wrong still turns out fine
questions.explanation: All valuation is uncertain. The margin of safety is the buffer between price and estimated value that absorbs your errors — the core idea of value investing.

questions.text: A backtest accidentally uses each day's closing price to decide a trade entered that same morning. This bug is called:
options: Lookahead bias — using information unavailable at decision time; the #1 silent backtest killer
questions.explanation: Any leak of future information into past decisions inflates results invisibly. Guarding against lookahead is the first discipline of backtesting.

questions.text: Your strategy shows amazing results after tuning 12 parameters on 3 years of data. The likely reality:
options: The rules have memorized historical noise (overfitting) — validate with out-of-sample and walk-forward testing before believing it
More parameters always mean more robustness
It will work exactly as backtested
questions.explanation: Enough knobs will fit any historical dataset perfectly and fail live. Out-of-sample and walk-forward validation are the honesty checks.

questions.text: What is the FIRST step in the fixed chart-reading order?
options: Zoom out to the weekly/monthly chart for the multi-year context
questions.explanation: Context first: weekly/monthly story → daily trend structure → levels → volume → candles at key spots → indicators last. Starting at indicators is the classic inversion.

questions.text: Price pierces above a well-watched resistance intraday, finds no follow-through, and closes back below it. This false break is:
options: A buy signal — the breakout started
One of the most tradeable events on charts — trapped breakout buyers must unwind, fuelling a move DOWN
questions.explanation: Everyone who bought the 'breakout' is now losing and sitting overhead as supply. Their forced exits fuel the reversal — the logic behind trading traps, and springs at support.

questions.text: How many touches does a trendline need before you should trust it?
options: Two to draw it, three to trust it
questions.explanation: Two points define a line — anything can connect two points. The third touch shows the market is actually respecting it.

questions.text: In a bull flag, what should volume do during the flag (the pullback phase)?
options: Shrink — quiet profit-taking, not urgent selling; then expand again on the breakout
questions.explanation: The tell that a pullback is rest rather than reversal is drying-up volume. Expanding volume on the down-leg suggests distribution instead.

questions.text: You entered a swing trade off a daily-chart setup. It moves against you, so you switch to the 15-minute chart to find reasons to stay in. This is:
options: Timeframe demotion — the timeframe that put you in is the only one allowed to take you out
questions.explanation: Hunting a lower timeframe for hope is rationalizing a losing position. The daily setup defined the trade and its stop; the daily chart judges it.

questions.text: Roughly what share of a typical stock's daily move is explained by the overall market and its sector rather than the company itself?
options: Around three-quarters — which is why the tide matters more than the boat
questions.explanation: Most of a stock's move is market + sector. Great chart reads fail in bad markets, and mediocre setups work in strong ones — hence: market state first, stock second.

questions.text: The index makes a new high while the % of stocks above their 200-DMA makes a lower high. This divergence means:
options: Nothing — the index is all that matters
The army is thinning behind the flag — a classic late-cycle breadth warning that has preceded most major tops
A guaranteed crash within a week
questions.explanation: Fewer soldiers backing each new advance = a narrowing rally. Not a timing signal on its own, but a warning to reduce aggression and watch structure.

questions.text: FMCG, pharma and IT (defensives) start strongly outperforming while the index is still near highs. The market-reading interpretation:
options: Institutions are rotating into safety — the crowd is scared even though the index hasn't fallen yet
A signal of maximum risk appetite
Defensives lead only in bull markets
questions.explanation: Money hiding in stable-earnings sectors is defensive behaviour wearing a bullish mask. Sector rotation often tells the truth before the index does.

questions.text: The most useful way to read FII flow data is:
options: React to every single day's number
Track the ~20-day cumulative flow — one day is noise; a month of one-sided flow is a trend
questions.explanation: Sustained multi-week FII selling has accompanied nearly every meaningful Indian correction; single-day figures whipsaw. Cash-market cumulative flow is the signal.

questions.text: Very low India VIX (~10–12) for weeks means:
options: Complacency — often the fuel for shocks; also when buying options (protection) is cheapest
questions.explanation: Low VIX = the market prices in very little risk. That calm itself is information: protection is cheap, positioning is relaxed, and surprises hit harder.

questions.text: What does the JIT compiler do?
options: Compiles C# source code into IL at build time
Translates IL into native machine code at runtime, method by method on first call
questions.explanation: The C# compiler produces IL in assemblies; the CLR's Just-In-Time compiler turns that IL into native code as methods are first executed.

questions.text: Inside a catch block, what is the difference between `throw;` and `throw ex;`?
options: `throw;` rethrows preserving the original stack trace; `throw ex;` resets the stack trace, destroying the debugging trail
questions.explanation: `throw ex;` makes the exception appear to originate at the rethrow site. Use `throw;` (or wrap with InnerException) to keep the trail.

questions.text: A struct is assigned to another variable and one field of the copy is changed. What happens to the original?
options: The original changes too — they share memory
Nothing — value types copy by value, so the two are independent
questions.explanation: Value types (structs) copy their entire data on assignment. Reference types would share the same object — this distinction underpins the whole .NET memory model.

questions.text: Why expose an event instead of a public delegate field?
options: An event lets outside code only subscribe/unsubscribe (+=/-=) — it cannot invoke the handler chain or overwrite other subscribers
questions.explanation: A public delegate field could be invoked or reassigned by anyone, breaking the publisher's control. The event keyword restricts access to subscription only.

questions.text: Why does the GC collect Gen 0 far more often than Gen 2?
options: Most objects die young — collecting the newest generation frequently reclaims the most memory for the least work
questions.explanation: The generational hypothesis: short-lived objects dominate. Cheap, frequent Gen 0 collections handle them; expensive full (Gen 2) collections stay rare.

questions.text: In the middleware pipeline, why must UseAuthentication come before UseAuthorization?
options: Authorization checks the user that authentication established — reversed, every request is anonymous and gets rejected or passed wrongly
questions.explanation: Authentication answers 'who are you' and populates HttpContext.User; authorization answers 'are you allowed'. Order defines semantics in the pipeline.

questions.text: Why is DbContext registered as Scoped rather than Singleton?
options: DbContext is not thread-safe and tracks entities — one instance per request gives an isolated unit of work; a singleton would be shared across concurrent requests and leak tracked entities
questions.explanation: Scoped = one context, one change tracker, one implicit unit of work per HTTP request — matching web semantics and avoiding thread-safety crashes.

questions.text: What is a captive dependency?
options: A NuGet package with a restrictive license
A scoped/transient service injected into a singleton — the singleton holds that one instance forever, breaking its lifetime
A service that can't be mocked
questions.explanation: The singleton 'captures' the shorter-lived service. Fix: inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per operation.

questions.text: async/await improves web server scalability because…
options: await makes the database respond faster
an awaited I/O call releases the thread back to the pool, so the same threads serve many more concurrent requests
async methods run on the GPU
it doesn't — it's only for UI apps
questions.explanation: The request isn't faster; the server survives concurrency. Blocking with .Result holds threads through I/O waits and collapses throughput under load.

questions.text: appsettings.json sets Logging level to Warning; an environment variable sets it to Debug. What wins?
options: The environment variable — later configuration providers override earlier ones
Neither — it throws a conflict error
questions.explanation: Configuration is layered: appsettings.json → per-environment JSON → user secrets → environment variables → command line, with later sources overriding.

questions.text: Calling setCount(count + 1) twice in one click handler increments once. Why?
options: Updates are batched and both calls closed over the same stale count — use the functional form setCount(c => c + 1)
onClick only allows one state update
The component must be a class
questions.explanation: Both calls compute stale+1 from the same captured value. The functional updater receives the latest state and composes correctly.

questions.text: Why is the array index a bad key for list items?
options: On insert/remove/reorder, item identity shifts position — component state (inputs, selection) sticks to positions instead of items
questions.explanation: Keys let reconciliation track items across renders. Index keys break identity when the list changes shape — the classic 'typed text jumped to another row' bug.

questions.text: What is the cleanup function returned from useEffect for?
options: Undoing the effect (unsubscribe, clear timers, abort fetches) — it runs before each re-run and at unmount, preventing leaks and race conditions
questions.explanation: Each effect execution pairs with a cleanup. Miss it and you leak subscriptions/timers and let stale async results overwrite fresh ones.

questions.text: Why must hooks be called unconditionally at the top level?
options: React identifies each hook by call order per render — a conditional call shifts the order and every later hook reads the wrong state slot
Hooks are slow inside if statements
questions.explanation: Hook state is positional. Same order every render is the contract that makes useState/useEffect work at all — hence the lint rule.

questions.text: React.memo on a child does nothing because the parent passes an inline object prop. Why?
options: The inline object is a new reference every render, so memo's shallow comparison always sees changed props — stabilize it with useMemo/useCallback
questions.explanation: memo skips re-render only when props are shallow-equal. New object/function identities defeat it — referential stability is the other half of the optimization.

questions.text: For a typeahead search box calling an API per keystroke, which RxJS operator maps keystrokes to HTTP calls correctly?
options: mergeMap — run all requests in parallel
switchMap — cancel the previous request; only the latest query's result matters
concatMap — queue every request in order
exhaustMap — ignore new keystrokes while a request runs
questions.explanation: switchMap unsubscribes the stale inner observable, preventing out-of-order results overwriting fresh ones. (Pair with debounceTime + distinctUntilChanged.)

questions.text: Why is the async pipe preferred over manual subscribe in components?
options: It's shorter to type, nothing more
It subscribes, renders emissions, works with OnPush, and auto-unsubscribes on destroy — eliminating the most common Angular memory leak
questions.explanation: Forgotten manual subscriptions keep components alive after destroy. The async pipe manages the whole subscription lifecycle for you.

questions.text: Why does initialization code belong in ngOnInit rather than the constructor?
options: The constructor is for DI wiring; @Input values aren't set yet — ngOnInit runs after inputs are bound
questions.explanation: Fetches or logic depending on inputs must wait until Angular has bound them — that's ngOnInit's contract.

questions.text: With ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush, a component's list doesn't update after items.push(newItem). Why?
options: push mutates the same array reference — OnPush checks input references; create a new array ([...items, newItem]) instead
questions.explanation: OnPush skips the component unless an input reference changes (or an event/async pipe fires inside). Immutable updates are the required discipline.

questions.text: What does [(ngModel)]="qty" expand to?
options: A directive that watches the DOM with polling
[ngModel]="qty" (ngModelChange)="qty = $event" — a property binding plus an event binding
A WebSocket connection to the model
It's a special compiler primitive with no expansion
questions.explanation: Two-way binding is sugar: data flows in via property binding, out via the change event — the 'banana in a box' question.

questions.text: WHERE vs HAVING — which is true?
options: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation — SUM conditions can only go in HAVING
questions.explanation: Aggregates don't exist until GROUP BY runs, so conditions on them must be in HAVING; row-level filters belong in WHERE (cheaper — fewer rows reach the group stage).

questions.text: After LEFT JOIN Orders o, adding WHERE o.Status = 'Paid' does what?
options: Silently converts it to an INNER JOIN — NULL rows from unmatched customers are filtered out; put the condition in the ON clause to keep them
Makes it a FULL OUTER JOIN
questions.explanation: Unmatched left rows have o.Status = NULL, and NULL = 'Paid' is not true — so those rows vanish. Right-side filters preserve LEFT semantics only in ON.

questions.text: How many clustered indexes can a table have, and why?
options: One — the clustered index IS the table, physically ordered by its key; data can only be stored in one order
questions.explanation: The clustered index's leaf level is the data itself. Nonclustered indexes are separate structures pointing back to it — you can have many of those.

questions.text: WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2026 performs badly on an indexed OrderDate column because…
options: The function on the column makes the predicate non-SARGable — the index can't seek; rewrite as OrderDate >= '2026-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2027-01-01'
questions.explanation: The engine would have to compute YEAR() for every row. Keeping the column bare turns it into an index range seek.

questions.text: NOT IN (SELECT Email FROM Blocked) returns zero rows unexpectedly. The likely cause?
options: The subquery returns a NULL — with three-valued logic, NOT IN against a NULL can never be true; use NOT EXISTS instead
questions.explanation: x NOT IN (a, b, NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row. NOT EXISTS handles NULLs sanely and can short-circuit — the standard fix.
